title: Sharding
idea: Sharding splits a large dataset across several databases called shards. A partition key, such as a user id, decides which shard owns each row.

analogy.text: A phone book split into volumes by surname: A–F in one, G–M in the next. You pick the volume from the name before you look.
analogy.breaks: Rebalancing is harder: rows must be moved between running databases.

points: Each row lives on one shard, so writes and storage spread across machines.
Range sharding keeps nearby keys together; hash sharding spreads keys but scatters ranges.
A shard that gets far more traffic than the others is a hot shard.
A query without the partition key usually must ask every shard and merge results.

steps.caption: The app reads the partition key from the request, here a `user_id`, and picks one shard.
Range sharding gives each shard a block of ids: low, middle and high.
Ids keep rising, so every new user lands in the highest range. That shard runs hot.
Hash sharding hashes the key first, so the same new users spread across shards.
A query that does not include the partition key usually goes to every shard.
The app merges the answers. A query across shards costs more than one aimed at a single shard.

code.title: Range vs hash
code.caption: Six new, rising ids routed by range, then by hash. The output counts rows per shard.

pitfalls: Do not shard before simpler fixes fail; sharding adds real operational complexity.
Do not range-shard on a key that only rises, such as a timestamp.
Design queries around the partition key; cross-shard joins and transactions are costly.

quiz.why: Every id is 300 or more, so `Math.min(…, N - 1)` caps the shard at 2. All six writes hit the last shard.

takeaway: Sharding spreads data and writes; choose the key by how you query.

starters: What is the difference between sharding and partitioning?
How do I add a shard later without moving everything?
Can I use a database transaction across shards?
